messages.author: d00f6178fa8e05fe
messages.subject: double mixture model
parts:
Hi Stan,

I'm trying to implement model which can be find in Bayesian Cognitive Modeling book (Lee & Wagenmakers, 2014). You can find relevant part of the book on google books (http://tr.im/EdC7) starting on page 85.

We have matrix k[i, j] of people i and questions j. And we are expecting that there are two groups of people and two groups of questions. Each group of people is able to answer most of the questions from one group but not the other. Same goes for the other group of people. Now we want to identify membership to each group. There are two parameters which are discrete and used for mixing (x[i], y[i])... x[i] represents membership to group of people and y[i] represents membership to group of questions. For more details see the link above.



First problem

My Stan implementation is here (https://github.com/neekro/Stan_translate/blob/master/!TwoCountryQuiz_Stan.R). I'm not confident in it, but posteriors of alpha and beta are close to those implemented in Jags(and BUGS). But not close enough - that's the first issue here.  

Jags

         mu.vect sd.vect   2.5%    25%    50%    75%  97.5%

alpha      0.878   0.058  0.742  0.845  0.887  0.921  0.963

beta       0.059   0.039  0.008  0.031  0.049  0.078  0.155

Stan

                   mean se_mean    sd    2.5%     25%     50%     75%   97.5% n_eff  Rhat

alpha             0.910   0.003 0.088   0.665   0.878   0.936   0.971   0.997   716 1.000

beta              0.063   0.003 0.075   0.001   0.015   0.038   0.081   0.293   788 1.000


Second problem

l'll also need to extract posterior for x and y. In my model implementation I tried do it in generated quantities block in a similar spirit as I do it in simple mixture models, but it didn't work out. Any suggestions how to implement it? 


Regards,
Martin Smira
(University of Amsterdam)

messages.author: 3f22b207863d2049
messages.subject: Re: double mixture model
parts:
Hi Martin,

Looking at your code, it seems you are using discrete-valued parameters, which causes Stan's sampler to degenerate into a random walk. I'm also not sure you got the mixture model coded right. You are simply adding up log-probabilities, whereas one would expect something like "for i in 1:N increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(log(theta[i]) + lp_parts[i,1], log1m(theta[i]) + lp_parts[i,2])))". Here, index i represents an individual, and the second index represents a mixture component (a possible discrete outcome).

Maybe the code you have  is a result of literally translating JAGS/BUGS (which only uses conditional probabilities) to Stan (which requires the full joint posterior to be specified)?

You should drop all discrete parameters and marginalize over all possible (combinations of) discrete values in a loop, save the log-posterior in a temporary variable for each of those combinations, and then use log_sum_exp() and a vector of estimated probabilities (a simplex for each person) to weigh the log-posteriors of each mixture component. The estimates for the values of simplex will then tell you what the probabilities is in what group a person is. You may want to check the Stan manual chapter on mixture models as well. It has some example code.

Best,

Luc

messages.author: 368f61d9252655a2
messages.subject: Re: double mixture model
parts:
Luc,

Isn't that exactly what he is doing (well, implicitly)?

He is expressing the mixing weights as a product of two probabilities given by parameters x_prob and z_prob. Thus, the final mixing weights in the model are: (1-x_prob[i])*(1-z_prob[i]), x_prob[i]*z_prob[i], (1-x_prob[i])*z_prob[i] and x_prob[i]*(1-z_prob[i]). In the code, the term log(x_prob[i]) is written as bernoulli_log(1, x_prob[i]) and log(1-x_prob[i]) as bernoulli_log(0,x_prob[i]). The original model could be equivalently written as (the main difference is the function log_sum_exp, which should be numerically more stable than taking the exp +sum directly)

transformed parameters {
  vector[4] lp_parts[nx, nz];
  for (i in 1:nx) {
    for (j in 1:nz) {
      lp_parts[i, j, 1] <- (log1m(x_prob[i]) + log1m(z_prob[j]) + bernoulli_log(k[i, j], alpha));
      lp_parts[i, j, 2] <- (log(x_prob[i]) + log(z_prob[j]) + bernoulli_log(k[i, j], alpha));
      lp_parts[i, j, 3] <- (log1m(x_prob[i]) + log(z_prob[j]) + bernoulli_log(k[i, j], beta));
      lp_parts[i, j, 4] <- (log(x_prob[i]) + log1m(z_prob[j]) + bernoulli_log(k[i, j], beta));
    }
  }
}
model {
  for (i in 1:nx)
    for (j in 1:nz)
      increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(lp_parts[i,j]));
}

parts:
Silly me --- Martin is the one who is coding these models for Erik-Jan!
So I guess that one's not done yet. My question does still stand
about releasing the models. It'd be very helpful to Stan users.

The Google books link doesn't work --- it just appears to give
me pages unavailable in a Slavic language (doesn't look
like Dutch despite being on the .nl domain). But the pdf of the
first two parts, including the relevant pages, are available straight
from the authors:

https://webfiles.uci.edu/mdlee/LeeWagenmakers2013_Free.pdf

Do you know what the MCMC std error is for JAGS? And are you sure
it converged? The MCMC std err is reported under se_mean for Stan.
It'd be good to rule out sampling error as the source of any differences.

I'd also suggest simulating some data according to the model and fitting
that. Then you'd know if you're getting the right answers (to within
sampling uncertainty, of course).

As of yet, we haven't found models where we can't fit the same
answers as JAGS, which increases my confidence in both systems (though
Michael will probably scold me for saying so).

You definitely want to follow Herra Huu's advice and use log_sum_exp()
and log1m() for numerical stability and for efficiency.

And unless you need lp_parts in the output, I'd just define a single
lp_parts 4-vector as a local in the model and reuse it, replacing

transformed parameters {
vector[4] lp_parts[nx, nz];
for (i in 1:nx) {
for (j in 1:nz) {
lp_parts[i, j, 1] <- (log1m(x_prob[i]) + log1m(z_prob[j]) + bernoulli_log(k[i, j], alpha));
lp_parts[i, j, 2] <- (log(x_prob[i]) + log(z_prob[j]) + bernoulli_log(k[i, j], alpha));
lp_parts[i, j, 3] <- (log1m(x_prob[i]) + log(z_prob[j]) + bernoulli_log(k[i, j], beta));
lp_parts[i, j, 4] <- (log(x_prob[i]) + log1m(z_prob[j]) + bernoulli_log(k[i, j], beta));
}
}
}
model {
for (i in 1:nx)
for (j in 1:nz)
increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(lp_parts[i,j]));
}

with

model {
vector[4] lp_parts;

for (i in 1:nx) {
for (j in 1:nz) {

lp_parts[1] <- (log1m(x_prob[i]) + log1m(z_prob[j]) + bernoulli_log(k[i, j], alpha));
lp_parts[2] <- (log(x_prob[i]) + log(z_prob[j]) + bernoulli_log(k[i, j], alpha));
lp_parts[3] <- (log1m(x_prob[i]) + log(z_prob[j]) + bernoulli_log(k[i, j], beta));
lp_parts[4] <- (log(x_prob[i]) + log1m(z_prob[j]) + bernoulli_log(k[i, j], beta));
increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(lp_parts));
}
}
}

It'd be even more efficient without the bernoulli_log, taking
log(alpha), log1m(alpha), log(beta), and log1m(beta) outside the
loop and reusing inside the loop based on switching on the value of k[i,j].
It'd make the model even harder to read, though, so I wouldn't recommend it
unless you really need to scale this and it's not fast enough as is.

Why not just use x_prob and y_prob for inference? These are the probabilities
for the individuals and questions being in each class, and it's more efficient
to use probabilities for inference (posterior expectations) than samples (posterior
samples).

Otherwise, the model as coded in Stan above looks right to me (given Martin's
data and parameter declarations).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: double mixture model
parts:
I realized what the problem is. The "double mixture" part!

The overall model probability is

p(alpha,beta,x,z,theta,k)
= Uniform(alpha|0,1)
* Uniform(beta|0,alpha)
* PROD_{i in 1:I} Bernoulli(x[i] | 0.5)
* PROD_{j in 1:J} Bernoulli(z[j] | 0.5)
* PROD_{i in 1:I} PROD_{j in 1:J} Bernoulli(k[i,j] | x[i] == z[j] ? alpha : beta)

The problem is that you can't independently model the each (i,j) pair -- they
are all dependent through the x[i] and z[j]. That is, each x[i] applies
to all j in 1:J, and each z[j] needs to apply to all x[i] for i in 1:8.

There are 2^8 possible values for x and 2^8 possible values for z in
this tiny tiny example, but already that's 2^16, or about 64000, summands.

I don't think there's any way to code this model efficiently in Stan.
You can just sum over the 2^16 values of x, z, but that's going to be
very painful to code, slow to run, and not scalable. On the other hand,
it'll probably be more efficient at estimating the tails than the model
in JAGS.

- Bob

parts: On Aug 9, 2014, at 9:00 AM, Martin Šmíra <smira....@gmail.com> wrote:

> Is there a way in Stan to index high-dimensional arrays in chosen dimension?
> If you know what I mean. As in R or BUGS: x[5, 1:20, 5] extracting vector.

You can do this in Stan in the first dimensions, but not
arbitrary dimensions. So if the last two dimensions of x
were swapped, you can write head(x[5,5],20) for what
would be x[5,5,1:20] in R.

Generalizing these capabilities is on the to-do list.

Writing loops to do this in Stan is fast, though clunky. There's
no advantage to vectorizing assignnents in Stan --- just sampling
statements or other arithmetic going into log prob calculations
because it's involved in gradients, which can often be partially
evaluated (i.e., unfolded with the chain rule) in vectorized
operations.

- Bob
